lines.text: Father, in the name of Jesus, we pray for every son, every daughter whose father might have forsaken them.
I will pray for every father who has gone through the motions of running.
You are the Father who blesses Your children. Bless every child. Bless every father.

art.prompt: Night inside a small one-room home with deep teal walls. On the right third of the frame a small boy of about seven in a yellow shirt sits on a woven mat on the floor, holding a steel wristwatch loosely in his two open palms and looking down at it with a calm, relieved face. A single candle burns on a low wooden table beside him. Behind him a wooden door stands open and wide soft golden light pours through it and wraps around his shoulders like an embrace. The boy is the clear subject, gently lit; the mood is tender and safe, he is not alone.

Early evening on an earth road at the edge of a village of round mud huts with thatched roofs. In the centre, seen from behind and slightly to the side so his face is not visible, a man in a simple long cream robe kneels on one knee and lifts a small laughing girl of about five up in his arms. Two more children, a boy in a yellow shirt and a smaller girl in a patterned dress, run toward him with their arms stretched out. A warm lantern glows on a doorstep nearby and the last golden light of the sun rims the man's shoulders and the children's faces. Deep teal sky with the first star.

Night. On the right third of the frame a West African father in a faded green patterned shirt sits alone on the edge of a narrow bed in a small room with deep teal walls, shoulders bowed, eyes closed, holding a folded sheet of plain paper against his chest with both hands; the paper is folded shut and shows no writing. A single candle and a short pencil sit on a small wooden table beside him. A small yellow child's shirt hangs on a nail on the wall behind him. Soft golden light falls on his head and shoulders from a high window, like a hand resting on him. Large calm empty area of teal wall on the left.

trailer.say: Maybe you stopped the watch of your own. | You stopped *hoping.* You stopped crying.
He doesn't pretend the fathers may not *leave.*
It did not end with the one who *left.*

Listen to me, son, daughter: God *lifts* you up.

titles: When My Father Does Not Come Home | Day 2 · The Father Showed Up
The LORD Will Take Me Up: For Every Child Still Waiting
You Don't Have To Hold The Time Still
social.description:
Some fathers do not come home. David did not pretend otherwise, but his verse does not end with the one who left. It ends with the LORD, who takes a child up and holds him close.

THE WORD: Psalm 27:10 (read Psalm 27:7–14 aloud)
TONIGHT, children: listen to a clock for one minute and count sixty ticks. Then say quietly: “The LORD will take me up.”
TONIGHT, fathers: write “I am sorry” on paper, and under it what you are sorry for. Pray over it. Keep it. Send nothing yet.
SAY IT: The LORD will take me up.
social.pinned: What is one thing you want to start hoping for again? Write it below, and under it write: “The LORD will take me up.”
